title: LRU Eviction — Core Method
description: Least-recently-used eviction keeps the cache to its size limit by discarding whatever went unrequested longest: every hit moves the item to the front, every insertion pushes from the back. An ordered dictionary implements this in constant time per operation. LRU exploits temporal locality — recently used items are likely to be used again — which holds across most archive workloads. It is the default eviction policy for good reason: simple, fast, and usually right. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method.

title: LFU Eviction — Core Method
description: Least-frequently-used eviction counts accesses and discards the coldest items, which suits workloads where popularity is stable and a few records dominate. Frequency counters age over time so yesterday's hits do not squat forever. LFU beats LRU when the hot set is small and persistent — reference data, popular records — and loses when popularity shifts quickly. Choosing between them starts with measuring the workload's reuse pattern. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method.

title: Adaptive Replacement — Core Method
description: Adaptive Replacement Cache tracks both recency and frequency, maintaining ghost lists of recently evicted items to learn which policy the workload favors. When ghost hits show recency would have won, ARC shifts space toward the recency list, and vice versa. This self-tuning beats fixed LRU or LFU across mixed workloads without any manual knobs. ARC is the policy for caches that serve unpredictable, changing archive traffic. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method.

print("policy adapts toward whichever ghost list gets hits")

title: TTL Expiration — Core Method
description: Cached archive records go stale, so each entry carries a time-to-live after which it is treated as expired and re-fetched. TTLs vary by data class — volatile statistics get seconds, stable reference data gets hours — and every expiration is lazy, checked on access. Stale-while-revalidate can serve the old copy while refreshing in the background for latency-sensitive paths. TTL expiration is the standard answer to 'how do I cache without serving lies'. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method.
demo:
import time
store = {}
def put(k, v, ttl): store[k] = (v, time.time() + ttl)
def get(k):
    if k not in store: return None
    v, exp = store[k]
    return v if time.time() < exp else None
put("rec", "data", ttl=100)
print("fresh read:", get("rec"))
put("old", "stale", ttl=-1)
print("expired read:", get("old"))

title: Admission Filtering — Core Method
description: Not everything deserves cache space: admission filtering decides what enters, using a small sketch of recent request history to admit only items requested more than once. One-hit wonders — scanned once and never again — pass through without polluting the cache. TinyLFU-style filters give near-optimal admission in a few kilobytes of memory. Filtering on the way in is cheaper than evicting wisely on the way out, and the two compose well. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method.
